Consider a directed weighted graph G(V, E), where V is the set of vertices and E is the set of edges. Suppose we use adjacency list to implement the graph. Consider a sequence of |V| operations with each corresponding to a different vertex in V. For the operation for vertex v, the cost is assumed to be the number of outgoing edges from v.  (a) What is the cost of the worst possible single operation in this sequence of operations? (b) What is the average amortized cost of the above sequence of operations based on aggregate analysis?

message.content:
The worst possible single operation occurs when a single vertex has the maximum number of outgoing edges, which can be as large as |E| in the extreme case where all edges originate from one vertex. The average amortized cost is found by taking the total cost across all operations and dividing by the number of operations.

* The cost of the worst possible single operation is **|E|**, since the out-degree of a vertex v can be at most |E| (e.g., when all edges in the graph are outgoing from v), and the sum of all out-degrees equals |E|.

* The average amortized cost via aggregate analysis is **|E| / |V|**, because the total cost of the entire sequence is Σ_{v ∈ V} deg⁺(v) = |E|, and dividing this total by the |V| operations gives |E|/|V|.

The cost of the operation for vertex v is the number of outgoing edges from v, which is the out-degree of v, denoted as deg⁺(v).

The worst possible single operation would be the maximum out-degree over all vertices. In a directed graph with |V| vertices and |E| edges, the maximum out-degree of a single vertex can be at most |E| (if all edges emanate from a single vertex). So the worst case is |E|.

Wait, let me reconsider. In a directed graph, the maximum out-degree of a vertex is at most |V| - 1 (if we don't allow self-loops) or |V| (if we allow self-loops). But more generally, it can be at most |E| since the total number of edges is |E| and all could come from one vertex.

Actually, the maximum out-degree of any vertex v is bounded by |E| (since the sum of all out-degrees equals |E|, the maximum single out-degree is at most |E|). And this bound is tight if one vertex has all |E| edges as outgoing edges.

So the answer to (a) is |E|.

(b) Average amortized cost using aggregate analysis:
Aggregate analysis: We compute the total cost of the entire sequence of |V| operations and divide by |V|.

The total cost = sum over all v in V of (out-degree of v) = |E| (since in a directed graph, the sum of all out-degrees equals the total number of edges).

So the average amortized cost = |E| / |V|.
